title.narrative: Center for Investigative Reporting, core support, 2024-2027

description.narrative:
Stöd till CIN-strategi 2024-2027.
Under de kommande åren kommer Center for Investigative Reporting (CIN) att fortsätta att stärka medborgarna genom verifierad information om korruption och missbruk av makt på alla nivåer i Bosnien och Hercegovina med samma kraft och nivå av engagemang. Kontinuerliga ansträngningar kommer att göras för att säkerställa större ansvarsskyldighet myndigheter och institutionella företrädare i kampen mot korruption, genom förbättring av rättsliga och institutionella ramar och lagföring av dem som är inblandade i korrupta aktiviteter. CIN:s övergripande bidrag till detta mål definieras enligt följande: Den lagstiftande och institutionell ram kommer att förbättras för att effektivt bekämpa korruption och säkerställa lika tillgång till lag och rättvisa för alla medborgare. För att uppnå detta mål har CIN identifierat två huvudresultat av sitt arbete, vidare uppdelad i steg och resultat, vilka presenteras i resultatmatrisen. Utfall I definieras enligt följande: Medborgare har tillgång till verifierad information om korruption i den offentliga sektorn. Resultat II definieras enligt följande: Offentliga tjänstemän är redo att förbättra det juridiska och institutionella ramar i kampen mot korruption

Support to CIN Strategy 2024-2027.
In the coming years, the Center for Investigative Reporting (CIN) will continue to empower citizens through verified information about corruption and abuse of power at all levels in Bosnia and Herzegovina with the same vigor and level of engagement. Continuous efforts will be made to ensure greater accountability of authorities and institutional representatives in the fight against corruption, through the improvement of legislative and institutional frameworks and the prosecution of those involved in corrupt activities. CIN’s overall contribution to this goal is defined as follows: The legislative and institutional framework will be improved to effectively combat corruption and ensure equal access to law and justice for all citizens. To achieve this goal, CIN has identified two main outcomes of its work, further broken down into steps and results, which are presented in the Results Matrix. Outcome I is defined as follows: Citizens have access to verified information about corruption in the public sector. Outcome II is defined as follows: Public officials are ready to improve the legal and institutional framework in the fight against corruption

sector.narrative: Media and free flow of information

description.narrative:
Outcome I: Citizens have access to verified information about corruption in the public sector During the reporting period, Jan 2025 - Dec 2025, CIN exceeded its annual production targets and continued to demonstrate strong investigative and editorial capacity. This sustained production contributed to increased public access to verified information on corruption, abuse of office, and misuse of public resources. It strengthened transparency and public scrutiny of public institutions, while providing citizens, civil society, and competent authorities with evidence-based information to support accountability efforts.
CIN published: 25 investigative stories38 follow-up/news stories linked to investigations12 video stories184 short animated videos119 infographics and illustrations. These outputs contributed to making complex corruption cases more accessible and understandable to a broader audience through diversified multimedia formats. Several investigations also contributed to institutional and judicial follow-up, including investigations, indictments, verdicts, sanctions, and procedural changes linked to issues raised through CINs reporting. CIN's investigations also generated tangible accountability outcomes, contributing to 1 official investigation, 5 indictments, 6 court verdicts, 7 sanctions or suspensions, and 2 procedural or regulatory changes, demonstrating the continued relevance of investigative journalism in supporting institutional and judicial action against corruption.
The organization also updated three major public databases: Politicians Assets DatabaseProperty Holdings of Judges and Prosecutors DatabaseBiH Pardons Database.
These updates improved public access to structured and searchable information on the assets and activities of public officials and other areas relevant to corruption risks. They enabled citizens, journalists, and civil society organisations to independently access, analyse, and use verified data to support oversight, investigative work, and public accountability. In addition, CIN produced one publication/policy paper and organized four round tables aimed at increasing dialogue between civil society, professional communities, and institutions. These activities contributed to increased dialogue and exchange between civil society, professional communities, and public institutions on issues related to corruption and accountability. They also supported the use of evidence and investigative findings in discussions on policy, oversight mechanisms, and anti-corruption measures. CINs content achieved significant public outreach and visibility. Investigative content was republished 412 times by other media outlets, including online portals, television, and radio stations, confirming CINs continued relevance and credibility within the media landscape. This indicates that media actors increasingly rely on CIN as a trusted source, contributing to wider dissemination of verified information and increased public awareness of corruption issues.
CIN investigations continued to generate concrete institutional and judicial responses. According to the last narrative report, during the reporting period, CINs reporting contributed to: 1 official investigation5 indictments6 verdicts7 sanctions/suspensions2 amendments or procedural changes3 awards and recognitions. These responses demonstrate that law enforcement and judicial actors are acting on evidence presented through CINs reporting, reflecting increased institutional responsiveness to corruption cases.
Examples include investigations and prosecutions linked to misuse of public funds, corruption in public administration, organized crime, and abuse of official positions. Judicial and law enforcement institutions continued to verify allegations raised through CIN reporting, demonstrating the practical relevance and credibility of the organizations investigative work. This suggests that verified information produced by CIN is not only informing the public but also being used in formal accountability processes.
Outcome II: Public officials are ready to improve the legal and institutional framework in the fight against corruption CINs investigative work continued to trigger institutional responses and contributed to increased public pressure for accountability and reform. This public pressure has contributed to changes in how some institutional actors respond to corruption cases.
Authorities reacted to several investigations through the opening of investigations, filing of indictments, court proceedings, sanctions, and procedural changes. This indicates that law enforcement and judicial actors are increasingly taking action based on publicly available evidence, reflecting a degree of improved responsiveness and accountability practices. CINs findings also contributed to discussions on improving transparency, oversight mechanisms, and accountability practices in public institutions. These discussions suggest gradual shifts in priorities among certain institutional and professional actors toward strengthening accountability mechanisms.
The organization further strengthened cooperation with civil society representatives and professional communities through round tables and public discussions aimed at collectively advocating for institutional reforms and anti-corruption measures. This has contributed to stronger collaboration between actors advocating for reform, potentially increasing collective influence on institutional practices.
While legislative and institutional reforms remain dependent on broader political dynamics outside CINs direct control, the evidence demonstrates that CINs reporting continues to serve as an important catalyst for accountability processes and institutional reactions. However, changes at the legislative and high-level political level remain limited, indicating that some key actors have not yet shifted their priorities toward structural reform.
